chunks: And from him, from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

"The Mudabbir (a slave manumitted upon the owner's death) is a slave, and his master may revoke the manumission if he wishes: he may sell him, or if he wishes, give him away as a gift, or if he wishes, marry him off."

He (the Imam) said: "And if his master leaves him in the state of Mudabbir and does not introduce a change in him until the master dies, then the Mudabbir is free when the master dies. And from the third (of the estate), it is only like a man who made a will, then changed his mind later and altered it before his death; and if he left it and did not alter it until he died, it is taken according to it."

key_terms.الثُّلُثِ: The third (of the estate for bequests)
key_terms.الْمُدَبَّرُ: Mudabbir: A slave manumitted upon the owner's death

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling for a slave designated as Mudabbir if the owner dies without revoking the manumission?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal nature of *Tadbir* (conditional manumission) by defining the slave as still owned during the master's life, allowing the master to revoke the status through sale, gift, or marriage. It draws a precise analogy to a revocable bequest (*Wasiyya*), establishing that if the master dies without altering the status, the manumission is executed from the one-third share of the estate, reflecting the Shia juristic view that it is not an absolute transfer of ownership until death. This ruling underscores the flexibility of the master's control over the slave's status prior to death, distinguishing it from immediate emancipation.
